title: Internal consistency: α, ρA and ρC
summary: Cronbach's α, ρA and composite reliability ρC all estimate how consistently a reflective construct's indicators measure it, under different assumptions.

body.text: [[cronbachs-alpha]] assumes all indicators load equally (tau-equivalence); with unequal loadings it tends to underestimate reliability. [[rho-c]], composite reliability, uses the estimated loadings; with classic PLS it tends to overestimate reliability because PLS loadings are inflated. [[rho-a]] (Dijkstra & Henseler 2015) usually lies between the two and is the reliability that PLSc uses.

body.explanation: λᵢ are the standardised loadings. The numerator is the variance due to the construct, the second term in the denominator is the error variance of the indicators.

body.caption: Change the loadings and watch α, ρC and AVE. With equal loadings α and ρC coincide.

body.text: Hair et al. (2022) treat .70–.90 as satisfactory (.60–.70 acceptable in exploratory research) and values above .95 as a sign of redundant items or patterned responding. They are heuristics. All three measures apply only to reflective constructs. In the TAM example PEOU has α = .830, ρA = .834 and ρC = .887.

mistake.title: Assuming higher reliability is always better
mistake.text: Values above .95 often mean the items are near-paraphrases and the construct is measured narrowly. And none of these measures is meaningful for a formative index.

tryIt.task: Run the TAM example and open the reliability table. Compare α, ρA and ρC for each construct, then switch to PLSc and compare ρC again.

checks.question: Three indicators all load .80. What is ρC?

options.feedback: Correct: (2.4)² = 5.76; error = 3 × (1 − .64) = 1.08; 5.76 / 6.84 ≈ .842. With equal loadings α gives the same value.
ρC is not the average loading; combining items raises reliability above that of a single item.
.64 is one item's reliability (λ²), not the reliability of the three-item composite.
Check the error term: each item contributes 1 − .64 = .36 of error variance.

checks.explanation: Reliability of a sum rises with the number of good items.

checks.question: With classic PLS you often see α ≤ ρA ≤ ρC. Why is ρC typically the highest?

options.text: It is computed from PLS loadings, which tend to be inflated for reflective constructs.
options.feedback: Correct. Inflated loadings make the construct seem to explain more variance than it does.
That is α's assumption, which makes α conservative when loadings differ.
All three measures are block-level; structural paths play no role.

checks.explanation: Know the assumption behind each coefficient.
